identity.affiliation: Stockholm School of Economics (Swedish House of Finance)
identity.note: All three profiles recognize him with high confidence as the Swedish financial economist at the Stockholm School of Economics and Swedish House of Finance. Only A says he was earlier on the faculty of the University of Chicago Graduate School of Business and directed the Swedish Institute for Financial Research (SIFR). On committee service, A says several years (start uncertain, possibly early 2010s), G says longtime member and former chairman, and O gives no detail beyond the 2026 membership.

representative_works.title: Conflicts of Interest and Market Illiquidity in Bankruptcy Auctions: Theory and Tests
representative_works.contribution: Theory and tests using Swedish auction-based bankruptcy data. Shows frequent salebacks to former owners, consistent with market illiquidity and creditor conflicts of interest.

representative_works.title: Financial Contracting Theory Meets the Real World: An Empirical Analysis of Venture Capital Contracts
representative_works.contribution: Documents how actual VC contracts separately allocate cash-flow, control, voting, board and liquidation rights, often contingent on performance. This is consistent with incomplete-contracting and agency theories.

representative_works.title: Characteristics, Contracts, and Actions: Evidence from Venture Capitalist Analyses
representative_works.contribution: Uses VCs' internal investment memos to link perceived risks to contract terms. Assesses the roles of screening, contracting and monitoring in resolving agency problems.

representative_works.title: Leveraged Buyouts and Private Equity
representative_works.contribution: Widely cited synthesis of how PE creates value through financial, governance and operational engineering. Also reviews evidence on returns and boom-bust cycles.

representative_works.title: Why Are Buyouts Levered? The Financial Structure of Private Equity Funds
representative_works.contribution: Theory explaining fund-level equity combined with deal-level debt in PE as a response to agency problems between GPs and LPs.

representative_works.title: Which CEO Characteristics and Abilities Matter?
representative_works.contribution: Uses detailed assessments of CEO candidates in buyout and VC deals to relate personality and ability traits to selection and performance.

representative_works.title: Borrow Cheap, Buy High? The Determinants of Leverage and Pricing in Buyouts
representative_works.contribution: Shows that buyout leverage tracks credit-market conditions rather than firm-level determinants, and that higher leverage goes with higher prices.

representative_works.title: Private Equity and Industry Performance
representative_works.contribution: Finds that industries with more PE activity grow faster and are less volatile, without evidence of negative spillovers.

representative_works.title: Private Equity and Financial Fragility during the Crisis
representative_works.contribution: Studies how PE-backed firms fared during the financial crisis, bearing on whether PE ownership increases vulnerability or improves resilience.

representative_works.title: Since you're so rich, you must be really smart: Talent and the finance wage premium
representative_works.contribution: Uses Swedish registry data to argue that the rising finance-sector wage premium is largely driven by increased sorting of cognitive and non-cognitive talent into finance.
representative_works.conflict: G gives no year or venue. A and O do not list this work.

persona.summary: An empirical corporate finance economist whose signature contribution is confronting financial contracting theory with detailed contract- and deal-level data. He is a leading authority on private equity, venture capital, buyouts and bankruptcy, and he bridges microeconomic contract theory and real-world financial institutions.
persona.research_lens: He sees finance through incentive and contracting problems: agency conflicts, control rights, incomplete contracts and information asymmetry, and the institutions that address them (VC contracts, PE fund structures, bankruptcy procedures). Inferred from his record, he would read candidate work in terms of mechanism and institutional design: who holds control, what incentives contracts create, and what real consequences follow.
persona.methods_and_evidence: His work relies on theory-guided empirics using granular, often hand-collected or proprietary micro data. Examples are VC term sheets and investment memos, buyout deal leverage and pricing data, Swedish bankruptcy auctions, firm and industry outcomes, and (per G) Swedish administrative registers. These are combined with targeted formal models, plus influential synthesis surveys.
likely_questions_in_deliberation: Has the theory been confronted with real contracts or institutional data, and does it survive?
Does the empirical work identify the underlying mechanism, or merely show a correlation?
Are the contracts, institutions and legal or market settings modeled realistically, and is the data granular enough to reveal the frictions at play?
How robust is the evidence to selection into financing arrangements or ownership structures?
Does the work distinguish financial gains from real productivity, employment or welfare effects?
Did the contribution create a durable, broadly influential agenda, including for policy and practice, rather than document a single episode?
How does the work relate to earlier prizes in finance and contract theory, and is it distinct enough?
persona.committee_experience: He has served on the committee for multiple prize cycles (A, G) and is a member in 2026. A suggests this plausibly spans the 2013, 2016 and 2022 finance- and contract-related prizes. G alone states he previously chaired the committee and played a central role in the scientific backgrounds for the 2016 and 2022 prizes; A is explicitly unsure about his authorship of background documents. O gives no detail on length of service.
persona.support_note: The research lens, methods and values are shared by all three profiles. The committee-experience claims diverge: G's chairmanship and background-document authorship are uncorroborated. A is uncertain, and O declines to state service length. Recent-interest emphasis also diverges: A and O stress continuing PE and buyout work, while G stresses talent allocation and the finance wage premium, and ESG in private equity.

disagreements: Committee history: G says he is a veteran member who previously served as chairman and centrally shaped the 2016 and 2022 scientific backgrounds. A says he served multiple cycles, possibly from the early 2010s, but is unsure of roles and authorship. O has no independent information. The chairmanship claim is single-source.

Recent interests: A and O emphasize PE performance, leverage and real effects. G instead lists talent allocation and the finance wage premium, and climate/ESG in PE. These are not mutually exclusive, but there is no overlap across profiles.
Title spelling: G writes 'Centennial'; the listed title reads 'Centencial', likely a typo.
Coauthor spelling: A writes 'Morten Sorensen' for the 2012 CEO paper and 'Morten Sørensen' elsewhere; O uses 'Sørensen'.
Recent-interest periods differ: A gives 2015–2024, O mainly 2019–2024, G 2015–present or 2020–present.
caveats: Knowledge cutoffs: A about 2024, O about June 2024, G late 2023. None covers 2025–2026 work.

Several recent interests are explicitly inferred from his established profile rather than from verified post-2020 publications (A and O say so). A's and O's low-confidence interest items should be treated as speculative.
No namesake issues: all three profiles identify the same SSE / Swedish House of Finance economist, and no entries were dropped.
The persona's evaluative tendencies are inferences from his research record, not evidence of his committee positions. Nothing here predicts his 2026 prize views.

A.identity_note: Per Strömberg is a Swedish financial economist, professor of finance and private equity at the Stockholm School of Economics and associated with the Swedish House of Finance. He was earlier on the faculty of the University of Chicago Graduate School of Business and directed the Swedish Institute for Financial Research (SIFR). He is known for empirical corporate finance on venture capital contracts, private equity and leveraged buyouts, and bankruptcy. He has served on the Economic Sciences Prize Committee for a number of years; the exact start date is uncertain to me, possibly early 2010s.

I am unsure of the exact year he joined the committee, his specific roles in particular prize years, and his authorship of scientific background documents. I have limited knowledge of his most recent papers (2021 onward) and their titles. I make no predictions about his 2026 views.
